subject: Science
theme: X-ray contrast agents and radiopacity in medical imaging
question_short_text: Why barium is used in X-ray examination of the stomach
text: Barium in a suitable form is administered to patients before an X-ray examination of the stomach, because:
options: Barium allows X-rays to pass through the stomach on account of its transparency to X-rays
Barium compound, like magnesium sulphate helps in cleaning the stomach before X-ray examination
Barium is a good absorber of X-rays and this helps the stomach to appear clearly in contrast with the other regions in the picture
Barium salts are white in colour and this helps the stomach to appear clearly in contrast with other regions in the picture
answerText: (c) Barium is a good absorber of X-rays and this helps the stomach to appear clearly in contrast with the other regions in the picture
explanation: Barium sulfate is a radiopaque substance that absorbs X-rays rather than allowing them to pass through. When ingested, it coats the stomach lining and appears white on X-ray images, creating stark contrast with surrounding tissues. This allows radiologists to visualize the stomach's structure and detect abnormalities.

research.summary: The key concept being tested is understanding radiopacity and how contrast agents work in medical imaging. Barium sulfate (BaSO₄) is chosen specifically because its high atomic number (56) makes it an excellent X-ray absorber. When patients ingest the suspension, it does not pass through the stomach walls (ruling out option a). The mechanism is purely physical: barium's high atomic weight causes it to attenuate X-rays strongly, making the coated stomach appear bright white on the radiograph while surrounding soft tissues appear gray. This creates the necessary contrast for visualization. A common trap is confusing whiteness with reflectance—option (d) suggests the white color is visually important, but the actual mechanism is X-ray absorption creating the image brightness, not light reflection. Another trap is thinking barium has a cleaning function like an antacid or purgative (option b), but its only role is diagnostic contrast, not therapeutic. The distinction is critical: barium's utility rests entirely on its atomic number and X-ray absorption coefficient, not on its chemical reactivity or bulk properties. This is why barium sulfate specifically is used—being insoluble, it passes through the GI tract unchanged without being absorbed, remaining radiopaque throughout the imaging window.
facts: Barium sulfate has been used as a contrast agent in medical imaging since 1910, when German radiologist Walter Bachem introduced it for gastrointestinal tract imaging.

Soluble barium salts (carbonates, chlorides, nitrates) are highly toxic to humans because they are absorbed and cause neuromuscular blockade, which is why barium sulfate's insolubility is essential for safe medical use.
